attribution.note: Marcus's own endorsed description of Sutton's thesis, in his own newsletter.

semantics.note: The sentence's main clause says what Sutton's thesis was (always scaling, never hand engineering). The 'overstated' opinion is only a parenthetical. The drafter makes the opinion the assertion and takes the characterization as given. The contract rightly scores the characterization instead.

contract.note: Reading 'always' and 'never' at face value is the ordinary reading of Marcus's own categorical words. Scoring the factual characterization apart from his opinion is fair. The opinion itself cannot be tested.

evidence.note: A faithful institutional copy of the dated 2019 essay. It says human knowledge brings improvements in the shorter term and frames computation's advantage as 'ultimately' and 'in the long run'. It is not a claim that progress never comes from hand engineering.

reviews.rationale: The essay itself grants that human-knowledge methods help in the short term and limits its claim to long-run effectiveness. That meets the contract's contradiction condition, so Marcus's categorical 'never from hand engineering' misdescribes the thesis. His opinion that it is overstated is not scored.

attribution.note: Marcus's own endorsed claim about Hassabis's views.

semantics.note: Faithful: Hassabis now shares Marcus's critique of LLMs. The surrounding text sets out the critique: limits of pure prediction, and scaling is not all you need.

contract.note: Reading the critique as 'LLMs have limits and scaling alone is insufficient' is ordinary given the context. Marcus himself names scaling as the dividing line. The 2025 window and the mixed rule are reasonable.

evidence.note: A Google post under Hassabis's name (May 2025). It says further breakthroughs are needed for AGI and describes the world-model work. This is his own stated view, the very thing at issue.
Original Lex Fridman transcript (July 2025). He puts it at about 50/50 whether scaling existing systems will be enough. That keeps scaling's sufficiency an open question.

Third-party transcript of the Sept 2025 All-In talk. He lists missing core capabilities and bets on one or two breakthroughs, but says scaling 'maybe' gets there. Limits are agreed, with a reservation kept.

reviews.rationale: What holds: Hassabis acknowledged major LLM limits and leaned toward needing new breakthroughs. What fails: he explicitly left open, at roughly 50/50, that scaling alone could be enough. The contract says agreement on limits alongside that reservation is mixed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own endorsed claim about LeCun's timing and priority.

semantics.note: Keeps 'first', 'fully coming around', 'his own, very similar critique' and the end-2022 cutoff.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into the critique-by-2022 part and the priority part is fair. What 'first' is measured against is unclear, and the contract flags this.

evidence.note: LeCun's June 2022 position paper, in a readable reproduction, has a section saying scaling LLMs is not enough. That establishes the critique before the end of 2022. It says nothing about who was first.
Sept 2022 ZDNET interview. LeCun says his broader criticism goes back years, which casts doubt on 'coming around'. It neither dates his LLM-specific position nor settles priority.

reviews.rationale: The by-end-2022 part is supported: LeCun's June 2022 paper rejects scaling alone. Nothing in the packet compares when others adopted the view, so 'first' can be neither confirmed nor refuted. The support condition needs both parts, and nothing meets the contradiction condition.

attribution.note: Marcus's own endorsed comparison of his position with Sutton's.

semantics.note: 'Would' here describes positions they hold, not a prediction. The relative-emphasis wording is kept.

contract.note: Comparing the stated research priorities in qualitative terms is the ordinary reading. No numerical weights are invented.

evidence.note: Sutton, Sept 2025 Dwarkesh transcript: RL is 'basic AI', set against LLMs that mimic people.
In the same transcript Sutton says LLMs lack real world models and predict what people say, not what will happen.
Marcus, 2021 interview: neurosymbolic hybrids are the first of his steps. This is evidence of his stated priority, not of his claim.
In the same interview Marcus calls for a model of the current situation and contrasts this with GPT-3. That shows his world-model emphasis.
InfoQ's 2019 intro describes Marcus and Davis arguing for symbolic world knowledge with basic elements built in. This backs the innate-structure part.

reviews.rationale: Both men stress world models and the limits of language prediction. Sutton puts RL at the center, while Marcus leads with neurosymbolic hybrids and built-in knowledge. Nothing in the packet contradicts any part of the comparison.
